claims.text: In situ aberration-corrected STEM equipped with a heating stage can directly reveal atomic-scale structural changes in heated nanoparticles.
Nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt, containing five elements, qualifies as a high-entropy alloy.
Heating AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will produce lattice distortions, incipient phase boundaries, and atomistic diffusion events observable by AC-STEM.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are synthesized at room temperature.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have uniform composition and a controlled size distribution.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles exhibit a stable, homogeneous FCC or mixed-phase lattice structure.
A dedicated in situ heating holder can gradually heat the nanoparticles from room temperature to approximately 800 °C while they are observed by AC-STEM.
A controlled heating environment can minimize oxidation and beam-induced damage while preserving atomic-scale resolution up to approximately 800 °C.
Lattice distortions, local phase boundaries, and atomistic diffusion mediate the structural evolution of the nanoparticles under thermal stress.
Increasing temperature causes thermodynamic contributions in the multimetal system to promote specific atomic rearrangements.
Temperature-driven atomic rearrangements lead to local lattice distortions and transient phase boundaries.
These microscopic rearrangements underpin enhanced thermal stability in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
At elevated temperatures, real-time AC-STEM imaging will show measurable lattice distortions and may show phase-boundary nucleation or enhanced diffusion.
At room temperature, the nanoparticles have a uniform, well-ordered lattice with minimal or no observable atomic rearrangements.
The method is most reliable up to approximately 800 °C, provided that oxidation and beam damage do not compromise resolution.
Direct experimental data are limited for the thermal behavior of high-entropy nanoparticles under the proposed conditions.
A lack of statistically significant lattice distortion, phase-boundary formation, or diffusion relative to the room-temperature baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial state permits a mixed-phase lattice, whereas the baseline and predicted contrast assume a uniform, well-ordered room-temperature lattice. A mixed-phase initial state would already contain phase regions or boundaries and would weaken that stated contrast.
